title: Mastering Scleritis: The Anterior vs. Posterior Paradigm
summary: An inflammatory, potentially vision-threatening condition affecting the scleral tissue, characterized by severe pain and complex systemic associations. Differential diagnosis remains paramount to distinguish scleritis from episcleritis and orbital pseudotumor.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Scleritis is a chronic, painful, inflammatory disorder of the sclera. It is characterized by edema and cellular infiltration of the collagenous scleral framework. Unlike episcleritis, it is frequently associated with life-threatening systemic autoimmune diseases, notably rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA).

sections.title: Red Flags: When to Panic
content: Severe 'boring' pain radiating to the temple or jaw.
Avascular areas in necrotizing scleritis (high risk of perforation).
Decreased visual acuity (posterior involvement).
Presence of systemic vasculitis symptoms (hematuria, dyspnea).
Poor response to topical NSAIDs.

rows: Disc edema, choroidal folds, exudative RD

sections.title: Pathophysiology & Etiology
content: Type III/IV Hypersensitivity reactions causing collagen degradation.
Immune-complex deposition in scleral vessels.
Systemic Associations: Rheumatoid Arthritis (most common), GPA (Wegener's), Relapsing Polychondritis, Polyarteritis Nodosa (PAN).
Infectious etiology: Herpes Zoster, Pseudomonas, Syphilis, Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup Process
content: Step 1: Thorough history (rheumatologic/infectious review).
Step 2: Slit-lamp exam (diffuse light vs. red-free light).
Step 3: Phenylephrine 2.5% test to distinguish from episcleritis.
Step 4: B-Scan Ultrasound (looking for retrobulbar edema).
Step 5: Systemic blood work (CBC, ESR, CRP, RF, ANCA, ACE, QuantiFERON).

content.explanation: T for 'Tenon's Capsule' fluid. In Posterior Scleritis, the T-sign on B-scan represents fluid in the sub-Tenon space creating a perpendicular appearance to the optic nerve.

rows: Involvement of extraocular muscles, usually unilateral pain.

sections.title: Treatment Protocol
content: 1st Line: Oral NSAIDs (Indomethacin 25mg TID or Naproxen 500mg BID).
2nd Line: Systemic Corticosteroids (Prednisone 1mg/kg/day).
3rd Line: Immunomodulatory therapy (Methotrexate, Mycophenolate Mofetil, or Rituximab for refractory GPA).
Surgical: Scleral patch graft for impending perforation (tectonic support).

sections.title: Key Clinical Pearls
content: Always perform a fundus examination to rule out subclinical posterior involvement.
Necrotizing scleritis without inflammation ('scleromalacia perforans') is highly characteristic of RA.
Always investigate the underlying systemic cause; the eye may be the 'window' to a life-threatening systemic vasculitis.
Avoid subconjunctival steroid injections in scleritis; they increase the risk of scleral melting.
